name: American Green
lede: American Green is a muted sage first plated by Ridgway in 1912, a color Gustav Klimt used nearly nine times more than his museums' baseline rate, despite its being filed under a place word on the other side of the Atlantic from Vienna.

sections.title: A place word, no documented story
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas plates this sage at plate XLI, hue 33 triple-prime, tone i, a scan of an aged plate treated here as approximate [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS circular later classed it as moderate yellowish green, 6.1 units from its block center, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary separately dates the name to 1905, plate 22 A7 [1]. The Munsell notation is 1.0G 5.5/3.1 [1]. Our sources classify "American" here only as a place word; nothing in the books consulted explains why this particular sage carries it [1].

The closest named color on screen is [[slate-green]], 2.8 units away and described as almost the same; [[green-grey]] follows at 3.3, read as yellower, [[sage-green]] at 4.4, lighter, and [[french-green]] at 4.8, greener and more vivid [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this sage in 1.01 percent of 23,781 paintings, 241 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in 111, as photographed [2]. That ranks it ahead of 60 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 22 of 1,674 paintings, present in 1.3 percent of the 1,674 paintings (22 of them) dated to that century, 2.5 times its museums' baseline rate [2].

Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, 29 percent of its 111 appearances by lightness rank, meaning it is more often tucked into shadow than shown plainly [2]. Gustav Klimt is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 6 of his 50 works, 8.7 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [2]; Camille Pissarro follows at 6.1 times, and the color is also over-represented in the Impressionist movement generally, 5.0 times its baseline [2]. It is further over-represented in Austrian painting specifically, 5.9 times the expected rate, 6 of 121 Austrian works, which lines up with Klimt's own home city [2]. The earliest match in our archive is a painting dated to 1401, 511 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name; that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not the pigment itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
